newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say ready in principle to start talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say ready in principle to start talks.

text.p: Marxist hostage-takers said on Saturday they were ready in principle to start direct talks with Peru's government but refusal to consider their demand to free jailed comrades was blocking negotiations.

Within a framework of discussing all issues, including the demand to free some 400 jailed rebels, "we are ready to converse as we were willing to since we occupied this diplomatic site," said a Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) spokesman via two-way radio.

However, the government's refusal to consider their principal demand means "there is no possibility of starting conversations because in practice they are asking us beforehand to drop our request, which signifies a formal call to surrender which we will never accept," he added.

In a five-point communique via two-way radio with local Radio Programas del Peru (RPP), the MRTA also accepted the government's proposal of a Canadian government representative on a "guarantor" committee overseeing the talks.

"The government proposal to include a representative from Canada is acceptable," said the spokesman assumed to be MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini speaking from within the besieged Japanese ambassador's home where 73 VIP hostages were held on Saturday for a 32nd day.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo said on Friday former hostage and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent would sit on the commission. Palermo also proposed meeting outside the residence but ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners.

"About the place of the meeting, we take note of the proposal and through internal channels we will respond. Through those means we will also specify better the role of the guarantors, because we believe all serious and responsible negotiation cannot be only through public communiques," said the rebel spokesman.
Immediately after the conversation, rebels held radios to a window of the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence as if to demonstrate the veracity of the conversation, RPP said.
The radio station only broadcast the last three of the five points in the communique.

Earlier, from Copenhagen, MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said the rebels would not agree to meet outside the residence. "A meeting has to be within the residence," he told Reuters by telephone from Copenhagen.
Velazco said the presence of observers was not enough to "guarantee the physical safety of the commander (Cerpa)."

The rebels inside the booby-trapped and mined compound in Lima launched a fresh propaganda offensive on Saturday, unfurling three banners that struck comparisons between their hostages, Peru's poor and their jailed colleagues.

"Most of the population would like to feed themselves as well as the authorities held here," read one message, referring to the meals provided daily by the Red Cross during the 32-day siege. "These differences justify the people's struggle."

On two more banners the rebels said the captive officials were "responsible for the government's policies that affect the people" and that the guerrillas' jailed comrades also had families that wanted freedom for their relatives.
Using night-vision lenses, local television showed rebels in the early hours scurrying across the building's roof and hanging down large, white sheets with neat black letters.
About half an hour later, three men came out again to erect their red and white MRTA flag that depicts a mace and rifle flanking the long-haired 18th century Indian revolutionary leader Tupac Amaru.

The MRTA has held onto those men it considers the best bargaining chips, including top government and security force officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori.
The government announced on Saturday the formation of a special support committee, consisting of eight mental health specialists, to give moral support to relatives of the hostages.

Velazco said in part the rebels held the Japanese captive as a deterrent to Fujimori using force to end the siege. "If they had been freed, Fujimori would by now have tried to occupy the residence militarily," the spokesman said.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he believed Peru chose Canada as a talks' observer -- and not Spain or Italy as suggested by the rebels -- to try to prevent the standoff spreading to Europe.
"Probably they want to keep it within the Americas," Hashimoto told reporters.
